e.etymology: A K- spelling of Crew, the English word for a team that works together, which became a boys' name in the 2010s.

assoc.t: krewe, a New Orleans Mardi Gras parade club

e.etymology: A pet form and phonetic spelling of Louis, the French form of Germanic Ludwig, built from words for fame and battle.

assoc.t: Louie Louie, the 1963 Kingsmen rock song
Louie, one of Donald Duck's nephews with Huey and Dewey
King Louie, the orangutan in The Jungle Book
Louie, slang for Louis Vuitton

e.etymology: A Hebrew name read as watchful, borne in the Bible by one of King David's officers. For girls it is also a Russian short form of Irina and a Sanskrit name.
namesakes: Ira Glass (host of This American Life)

assoc.t: IRA, individual retirement account
IRA, the Irish Republican Army

e.note: Spelled like the initials IRA (retirement account, Irish Republican Army); ira is also the Spanish word for anger.

e.etymology: From Arabic samir, a companion who shares evening conversation. The Indian name Sameer, Sanskrit for breeze, is often spelled the same way.
From Latin angelica, angelic, ultimately from Greek angelos, messenger. Ariosto made it famous as the heroine of Orlando Furioso (1516).

assoc.t: Angelica Pickles, the bossy cousin on Rugrats
Angelica Schuyler in the musical Hamilton
angelica, an aromatic herb

e.etymology: From Brixton, a district of south London, first recorded as the stone of Brixi, a Saxon lord. Its use as a first name is recent and mostly American.

assoc.t: Brixton, district of south London
The Guns of Brixton, song by The Clash

e.etymology: A form of Jenny, mostly used as a short form of Jennifer, the Cornish form of Guinevere. It took off in the US after the character Jenna Wade appeared on the TV series Dallas.
An American contraction of the English surname and place name Harland, from Old English words for hare or gray plus land.

assoc.t: Harlan County, Kentucky coal country

e.etymology: The English word sky, borrowed from Old Norse sky, cloud. It is a modern nature name and also a short form of Skyler.

assoc.t: Skye, the pilot pup in PAW Patrol (same sound)
SKYY vodka (same sound)
Chicago Sky, WNBA team

e.etymology: From Siena, the medieval hill city in Tuscany and home of Saint Catherine of Siena. Sienna, the double-n spelling, is also the English word for a reddish-brown pigment named after the city.

assoc.t: Siena, medieval city in Tuscany, Italy
Toyota Sienna minivan (same sound)
Siena College and its political polls

e.etymology: A Greek name tied to meli, honey, made famous by the actress Melina Mercouri. It also arose as a short form of names such as Carmelina and Emelina.
namesakes: Melina Mercouri (Greek actress, Never on Sunday)

assoc.t: Melina, the guide in the video game Elden Ring

e.etymology: From Greek thallein, to flourish. In Greek myth Thalia is the muse of comedy and also one of the three Graces.

assoc.t: Thalía, Mexican pop singer and telenovela star
Thalia Grace, daughter of Zeus in Percy Jackson

e.etymology: From Irish Conchobhar, Old Irish Conchobar, lover of hounds. Conchobar mac Nessa is the king of Ulster in Irish legend.

assoc.t: Conor McGregor, Irish UFC star

e.etymology: The Latin word for rose, and the form of Rose used in Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

assoc.t: Rosa Parks, civil rights pioneer
rosa, Spanish for rose and for the color pink

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English for the king's wood or clearing.

assoc.t: Ben Kingsley, Oscar-winning actor (surname)

e.etymology: A modern American spelling of Adeline, a French diminutive of Adele, from the Germanic word adal, noble. It gives a ready route to the nickname Addie.

e.meaning: pure, the traditional reading of Catherine
e.etymology: A modern spelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Catherine. English speakers began reading the Irish spelling as KAYT-lin in the 1970s, which produced many respellings.

e.meaning: noble, as a form of Alina
e.etymology: A spelling of Alina, a European short form of Adelina and similar names built on the Germanic word for noble. Aleena is also a Muslim girls' name in Pakistan and India, from Arabic through Persian.
A double-l, double-n spelling of Eliana, Hebrew for my God has answered, shaped by the popularity of Ellie and Anna.
From the name of the meadow plant, Old English clafre. A four-leaf clover is a symbol of good luck, and the shamrock ties the name to Ireland.

assoc.t: four-leaf clover, symbol of good luck
Clover, payment terminals used by shops and cafes
Clover, a spy on the cartoon Totally Spies!

e.etymology: From the Caspian Sea, named in Latin for the Caspi, an ancient people of its shores. C. S. Lewis used it for Prince Caspian in The Chronicles of Narnia.

assoc.t: Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water
Prince Caspian in The Chronicles of Narnia

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Latin Maximus, greatest, a Roman family name borne by several early saints.
A spelling of Hallie made famous by the actress Halle Berry, whose parents took it from Halle's, a Cleveland department store. Halle is also a German surname and city name.
namesakes: Halle Bailey (singer, star of The Little Mermaid)

assoc.t: Halle Berry, Oscar-winning actress

e.note: People who do not connect it to Halle Berry often read it as Hall or Hailey.

e.etymology: From Arabic sariya, a cloud that travels by night. In the US it also follows the fashion for -iyah names such as Aaliyah and Mariyah.
From Eirinn, a grammatical form of Eire, the Irish name for Ireland. Erin is a poetic name for the country, taken up as a given name outside Ireland in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Erin Brockovich (environmental activist, subject of the 2000 film)

assoc.t: Erin go Bragh, the Ireland forever slogan

e.note: Sounds the same as Aaron in most American accents.

e.etymology: From Greek Eirene, peace, the name of the goddess of peace, of early Christian saints and of an 8th-century Byzantine empress.
namesakes: Irene Cara (singer of Fame and Flashdance)

assoc.t: Hurricane Irene, which hit the East Coast in 2011
Goodnight, Irene, the folk standard

e.etymology: From Latin flos, flower. Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, and the name was long a favorite in Scotland.

assoc.t: flora, the word for plant life (flora and fauna)
Flora, the red fairy in Disney's Sleeping Beauty

e.etymology: The English word chosen, from choose, used as a name with a religious ring, as in the chosen one and God's chosen people. Its use as a given name is recent and American.

assoc.t: The Chosen, TV drama about the life of Jesus
the chosen one, the destined-hero trope

e.etymology: A modern American name that puts the -lani ending of Hawaiian names such as Leilani and Kailani on the sound of Ayla. It is also spelled Ailani.

e.meaning: wolf cub (Irish surname) or church canon (English surname)
e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: Irish O Canain, descendant of Canan, from cana, wolf cub, and English canon, a clergyman. As a first name it also echoes the artillery piece.

assoc.t: cannon, the large artillery gun
Canon cameras and printers (same sound)
Nick Cannon, TV host (surname)

e.etymology: From an English surname, taken up as a girls' name in the 2010s alongside the similar-sounding Kinsley and Kenley.

e.meaning: land left by a drained lake
e.etymology: From an English surname taken from Marlow in Buckinghamshire, whose Old English name describes land left after a pool drained. The playwright Christopher Marlowe made this spelling famous.

assoc.t: Christopher Marlowe, Elizabethan playwright (surname)
Philip Marlowe, Raymond Chandler's private detective
